clue.text: A slave of man and fate

parts.note: a man is referred to as he
one's lot is one's fate or destiny

explanation.surface: A slave reflects that he is the servant of both his master and destiny.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Sparta the serf class who worked the land were bondsmen, so the word now means any slave.

clue.text: Coin once designed for William or Mary?

definitions.text: Coin once designed for William or Mary?

parts.words: Coin once designed for William or Mary?
parts.note: William and Mary reigned jointly, so each could be said to wear only part of the royal headgear; the old coin worth two shillings and sixpence fits that picture

explanation.surface: A question about a coin minted in the reign of William and Mary.
explanation.walkthrough: William III and Mary II ruled England together, so each had half the crown. The coin of that name was worth two shillings and sixpence in British money before 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: A former British silver coin worth an eighth of a pound, named for a share of a monarch's headgear.

clue.text: In midgame one may recover from a slice

definitions.text: In midgame one may recover from a slice

parts.words: In midgame one may recover from a slice
parts.note: at half-time in a match players traditionally refresh themselves by sucking a sliced citrus fruit; slice suggests a golf shot

explanation.surface: A golfer who slices a shot may recover halfway through the round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slice' suggests a sliced golf drive; it is a slice of fruit sucked at half-time in football or rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: A sour yellow citrus fruit, cut into pieces handed to players at the interval.

clue.text: Without Ariadne he'd have been clueless

definitions.text: Without Ariadne he'd have been clueless

parts.words: Without Ariadne he'd have been clueless
parts.note: Ariadne gave the Athenian hero a ball of thread, the original clew, to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth

explanation.surface: A remark that a man would have been lost without Ariadne's help.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'clew' is a ball of thread, the origin of the word 'clue'; without Ariadne's thread the hero could not have left the labyrinth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian hero who slew the Minotaur escaped the maze by following Ariadne's thread.

clue.text: Hookah with main attachments

explanation.surface: A smoker's hookah comes with pipes connected to the main.
explanation.definitionFit: A hookah draws smoke through a bowl of liquid, and the conduits joined to a mains supply carry the household's liquid too.

clue.text: West hit by N.E. resort

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A northeastern seaside town is battered by westerly winds.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yorkshire coastal town, famous for its abbey and Dracula, is a holiday spot in northeast England.

clue.text: Beastly scrap of old-fashioned jazz

parts.note: a tiger is a wild beast
a rag is a scrap of cloth

explanation.surface: A nasty fragment of dated jazz music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' looks like an adjective meaning nasty; it stands for a beast. The answer is a classic 1917 Dixieland number.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous early Dixieland jazz standard first recorded in 1917.

clue.text: To end session without Liberal reform is ludicrous

indicators.note: without here has its old sense of outside, so one word goes around another

parts.note: Parliament or a court rises when it ends its sitting

indicators.note: to reform something is to make it over, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Ending a parliamentary sitting without Liberal reform would be absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking', but here it has its old sense 'outside'; 'reform' rearranges the short form of Liberal, and Parliament 'rises' when a sitting ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Something laughable or absurd provokes laughter.

clue.text: Perhaps enclose in the cheek

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters may form something else, signalling a rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hint that the cheek might be enclosing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cheek' looks like the face, but it is the definition in its sense of impudence; 'Perhaps' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheek is impudence, rude disrespect shown to someone.

clue.text: Long Island ? Near, but is under 45 inches

indicators.note: in a down answer one piece placed under another comes after it

parts.note: the old English ell was a cloth measure of 45 inches
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is Long Island close by, but shorter than 45 inches?
explanation.walkthrough: 'under' puts IS below ELL in this down light. The definition says the island is not Long Island but near it: it lies in New York Harbor.
explanation.definitionFit: The immigration island in New York Harbor lies close to that larger one.

clue.text: Horse-gunners toning-up

explanation.surface: Mounted artillerymen getting themselves fit for action.
explanation.walkthrough: A limber is the two-wheeled cart that horse artillery hitch a gun to; hooking it on is the gunners' task, and to limber up is also to stretch before exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: Horse artillery attaching guns to their two-wheeled carts are at that task, and stretching the muscles before sport is the other sense.

clue.text: Fibre is buried in salt

indicators.note: something buried in a place is put inside it, so one word sits within another

parts.note: sal is the old chemists' Latin for salt, as in sal volatile

explanation.surface: Some fibre has been left lying under a layer of salt.
explanation.definitionFit: The agave plant gives a strong natural strand used for rope and matting.

clue.text: Flowers we hear at the end of a pilgrimage

definitions.text: Flowers we hear at the end of a pilgrimage

parts.words: Flowers we hear at the end of a pilgrimage
parts.note: pilgrims in Chaucer's tales travel to a Kent cathedral city, whose ringing they would hear on arrival; the same name belongs to a tall blue garden campanula

explanation.surface: The sound of flowers greeting pilgrims as they arrive at their journey's end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' is not a sound-alike signal here: it means the ringing is what pilgrims hear on reaching the Kent cathedral of Chaucer's tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A campanula with bell-shaped blooms named after the Kent cathedral city, whose ringing ends the pilgrims' road.

clue.text: This rule should be No I in the book, said Alice

definitions.text: This rule should be No I in the book, said Alice

parts.words: This rule should be No I in the book, said Alice
parts.note: in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the King calls Rule Forty-two the most ancient in the book, and Alice replies that it ought then to be Number One

explanation.surface: Alice argues about which rule deserves first place in the rulebook.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'No I' is the page's 'No 1'. The King of Hearts claims his rule is the most ancient one in the book, and Alice retorts that it should then be Number One.
explanation.definitionFit: The rule the King names as the most ancient in the book is the one Alice says should come first.

clue.text: Address I've interpreted as an order

parts.note: to address a letter is to direct it
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A speech was taken as giving a command.
explanation.definitionFit: An official instruction is a command.

clue.text: Publican clubbed at Lord's

explanation.surface: An innkeeper is beaten up at a cricket ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is London's famous cricket ground, and the Lord's Taverners are a charity cricket club based there; 'clubbed' means made a member of that club, not beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: An innkeeper is a keeper of a tavern, and members of the charity cricket club at Lord's take the same name.

clue.text: British drive upsetting to foreigners

parts.note: British cars have the steering wheel on the side away from the kerb, which foreign drivers find awkward

explanation.surface: Visitors are unnerved by how the British drive.
explanation.walkthrough: British traffic keeps left, so British cars are built with the steering wheel on the offside, which confuses drivers from countries that keep the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: The steering position of a British car is on the side opposite the left.

clue.text: What's for pudding? The answer is a 2 possibly

indicators.note: possibly says the letters might be arranged another way, signalling a rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
2 refers to the solution of the clue at 2 down

explanation.surface: Asked what dessert is, someone says it might be a citrus fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges IS, A and the answer to 2 down. 'pudding' is the British word for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheat grain cooked in milk makes a traditional British school dessert.

clue.text: Where a gas in bed is natural

definitions.text: Where a gas in bed is natural

parts.words: Where a gas in bed is natural
parts.note: natural gas lies beneath the seabed off Britain's east coast, so the bed here is the floor of an ocean

explanation.surface: A coy remark about where it is acceptable to break wind in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The bed is the seabed and the gas is the natural gas found under the waters between Britain and Scandinavia in the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: The stretch of water east of Britain has natural gas fields beneath its floor.

clue.text: The case seems most comprehensive

parts.note: a travelling bag whose name says it takes everything is literally the most comprehensive piece of luggage

explanation.surface: A lawyer judges one legal argument to be the most thorough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' looks legal; it is a piece of luggage whose name says it takes everything.
explanation.definitionFit: A large soft travelling bag, so called because it carries everything.

clue.text: Good for nothing who commanded the Horse

parts.note: bade is the past tense of bid, so it means ordered or commanded
gee-gee is a child's word for a horse, abbreviated to GG

explanation.surface: A worthless officer once led a cavalry regiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Horse' looks like a cavalry regiment, but it is GG, the gee-gee of nursery talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotten person, worthless and unreliable, is called by this idiom.

clue.text: Pardon by which men stay in trouble, however

indicators.note: letters in trouble are thrown into disorder, so these words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pardon allows men to remain despite being in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' rearranges MEN STAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A general official forgiveness for offences is a pardon granted to many.

clue.text: Pasture overnourished with foliage

parts.note: lea is a poetic word for meadow or pasture
the word splits into over, placing one piece above the next in this down light, and nourished, which means fed

explanation.surface: Grassland given too much fertiliser grows lush leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overnourished' is read as 'over' plus 'nourished': LEA goes over FED.
explanation.definitionFit: Having leaves, as a plant in growth does.

clue.text: Pub regulation currently under review

parts.note: a British local is one's nearby pub
government is the regulating or ruling of something

explanation.surface: The rules for running pubs are being reconsidered.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the local' is one's neighbourhood pub. The definition is topical: the councils of England were being reorganised when this puzzle appeared, ahead of the 1972 Act.
explanation.definitionFit: Council administration in Britain was being reshaped at the time, so it was the thing currently being reviewed.

clue.text: They produce a rise in inland shipping

definitions.text: They produce a rise in inland shipping

parts.words: They produce a rise in inland shipping
parts.note: on a canal, gated chambers raise or lower boats between water levels

explanation.surface: Something is boosting the canal freight trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a rise' sounds like growth in trade; it is boats physically lifted between water levels on a canal.
explanation.definitionFit: Gated canal chambers lift barges from one level of water to the next.

clue.text: How weird that is — always first !

indicators.note: first says the word for always comes at the start, ahead of the other piece

parts.note: e'er is the poetic short form of ever, meaning always
i.e. abbreviates id est, that is

explanation.surface: An exclamation at how strange it is that something always comes first.
explanation.walkthrough: E'ER (always) is told to come first, ahead of IE (that is).
explanation.definitionFit: Strange and unsettling, giving a spooky feeling.

clue.text: Country is not all rich in a type of clay

indicators.note: the country is not all of the phrase that follows but only a part of it, its letters running inside those words

explanation.surface: A nation that is partly wealthy in a certain kind of clay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is not all' says the answer is only part of 'rich in a'. The closing 'type of clay' points to china clay, a second sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The large East Asian nation, whose name is also a white porcelain clay.

clue.text: Organisms that are Al for us in trouble

indicators.note: letters in trouble are thrown into disorder, so these words are rearranged

parts.note: the page prints A1, meaning first-rate, and its figure 1 is taken as the letter I
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Some creatures are perfect for us when things go wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' rearranges AIFORUS, with 'A1' (first-class) giving A and I.
explanation.definitionFit: These are microscopic protozoans, such as ciliates, found in infusions of decaying matter.

clue.text: Metal spar for balance

parts.note: steel is an iron alloy, a metal
a yard is the spar that holds a ship's sail

explanation.surface: A metal pole used to keep something level.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a weighing device with a long arm and a sliding counterweight, a kind of scale.

clue.text: Submit return

explanation.surface: A two-word command to surrender and bring back.
explanation.definitionFit: To give way is to submit, and the profit an investment produces is its return.
